1. The image compares two kinds of income payment, a level check and a rising check, using US consumer prices (CPI-U). It shows how inflation affects what each can buy. The chart is labeled "illustrative" and "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. Frame 1 draws a line for the rising check. It stays near the "first check" reference level from Aug 2006 to Aug 2026, with a small dip at the end. In frame 2 a second line, the level check, drifts steadily downward. Frame 3 marks year 5 on that line with the caption "about 9 in 10 by year 5." Frame 4 marks year 20 and adds "rising check: there after 20 years." Frames 5 and 6 add a question mark.

3. A level check pays the same dollar amount every year, so rising prices wear down what it buys. By year 5 it buys about 90% of what the first check did, and the line keeps falling after that. A rising check goes up with prices, so after 20 years it still buys about what the first check did. The question mark leaves open what to make of this.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. It shows the gap and ends on a question, so a viewer is left to decide for themselves.
